overview.body: BUILD unit. Module 4 opens by killing the hardest pain point from Module 3: those long lists of distance constants and parallel destination lists for every city. The city graph moves out of code and into two text files, loaded into dictionaries at startup. distances['San Antonio']['Houston'] returns 200. Adding ten more cities means adding ten more lines to a text file, not touching code. Everything else from Lab 3.3 carries forward unchanged: the main-menu loop, save and load, the play-again loop, the D20 travel mechanic, the hazard system, and the trip report file. Same game, smarter data shape.

mentorQuote.quote: Real codebases keep data and code in separate places. If you have to edit a function every time the business changes its mind about a city, the design is wrong. Move the data into a file, load it once at startup, and let the code stay still. That is the whole point of Module 4.

Add load_city_info(filename) that parses CSV lines into a dictionary of dictionaries with type and tagline keys
Refactor display_destinations, get_destination, and get_redirect in the library to take (city, distances) instead of parallel lists. Same function names, smarter data shape
Add is_win_city and is_dead_end helpers that read from the city info dictionary

Rebuild lab-4-1.py so the city graph is loaded from text files at startup. Keep the three-loop architecture (main menu, play-again, in-game), keep the D20 mechanic, keep the parallel-list hazards inline for now (they move to a file in Lab 4.2)
overview.keyConceptsText: Two new tools arrive together. .strip().split(',') is the standard CSV-parsing pattern from Chapter 8: .strip() removes the newline at the end of each line, .split(',') breaks the comma-separated values into a list of fields. Dictionaries (Chapter 9) replace parallel lists for any data shape where the keys are meaningful. A nested dictionary is just a dictionary whose values are themselves dictionaries: distances['San Antonio'] is itself a dictionary mapping destinations to miles. The in operator works on dictionaries too. 'Houston' in distances checks if Houston is a key. This is how the loader builds the nested structure: it checks if city1 not in distances: before creating the inner dictionary.
overview.textbookReference: Chapter 8 covers the string methods. Programs 8–1 through 8–14 demonstrate .strip(), .split(), and string traversal. Chapter 9 covers dictionaries. Programs 9–1 through 9–7 cover dictionary creation, access, the in operator with dictionaries, and looping through keys.

Inline parallel-list hazards still live in lab-4-1.py for this lab; hazards.txt arrives in Lab 4.2

content.body: A new function in function_library.py named load_city_distances(filename). It reads city_distances.txt one line at a time and builds a nested dictionary: the outer key is the starting city, the inner key is the destination, and the inner value is the distance in miles. Your game loads it at startup and reports how many cities it found.

Lab 3.3 declared one constant per route: SAT_TO_CORPUS = 150, SAT_TO_HOUSTON = 200, and so on. That works for three cities. It does not work for ten cities and twenty-four routes, which is what Module 4 hands you. content.quote: If you had to add twenty more cities to this game next unit, how long would it take? If the answer is 'just add twenty lines to a text file', the design is right. If the answer is 'edit the code in five places', the design is wrong. Pick the data shape that makes the next change small.

content.title: How the Road Network Is Modeled
content.body: The 24 routes in city_distances.txt are the cities you can drive between on a Texas interstate. San Antonio reaches Houston (I-10), Austin (I-35), Laredo (I-35), El Paso (I-10), and Corpus Christi (I-37). Houston reaches Galveston (I-45) and Dallas (I-45). Austin reaches Dallas and Fort Worth via the I-35E and I-35W split. Dallas and Fort Worth connect via I-30; Dallas reaches Texarkana via I-30; Fort Worth reaches El Paso via I-20 and I-10.

rows: Forgetting .strip()

Each line ends with a newline character. Without .strip(), the last field keeps it. Here the last field is the distance, which int() forgives, but in CP3 the last field is the tagline, and the hidden newline breaks every line that prints it. Use .strip() in both loaders.
Casting parts[0] or parts[1] to int
Only the distance is a number. City names are strings.
Skipping the if city1 not in distances: guard
The first time you see a city, distances[city1] does not exist yet, so distances[city1][city2] = miles raises KeyError.
Putting the function below the if __name__ block
Keep every library function above the test block at the bottom, where the others live. That block is only for running the library on its own.
Using with open(...)
That works too (Chapter 6 covers it), but these steps use open() and close(), so match them to keep your code aligned with later labs.

content.quote: Notice that the loader pattern is identical to the one you just wrote. Same .strip().split(','). Same per-line dictionary assignment. Different data shape on the output side, same parsing pattern on the input side. That is what good design feels like. The boring part is reusable.

info[city] = city_type stores a string, not a dictionary. You need info[city] = {'type': city_type, 'tagline': tagline}.
Quotes around the tagline

content.quote: When you refactor a function, keep the public name and shape stable if you can. The callers do not care what the function does inside. They care what they pass in and what they get back. display_destinations still prints a numbered menu and returns a count. The shape that gets passed in is different now. The shape that comes out is the same.

items: In function_library.py, find the DESTINATION HELPERS section from Lab 3.2.

Rewrite display_destinations(city, distances). First print the header print('From ' + city + ', you can travel to:'). It replaces the old Where would you like to go? line, because the menu now comes from the data file and names the city. Then set option_num = 1 and loop for dest in distances[city]:. Inside the loop, miles = distances[city][dest], then print(f' {option_num}. {dest} - {miles} miles') (two spaces before the number, same as before), then option_num = option_num + 1. After the loop, return len(distances[city]). The data file has no notes, so the (BEACH!)-style tags are gone.
Rewrite get_destination(city, distances, choice): dests = list(distances[city].keys()), dest = dests[choice - 1], and return (dest, distances[city][dest]).

Rewrite get_redirect(city, distances, avoid): options = list(distances[city].keys()), and remove avoid if it is in the list. Then handle both cases: if len(options) > 0: pick with index = random.randint(0, len(options) - 1) and dest = options[index], and return (dest, distances[city][dest]). else: the city has only the one route you just removed, so return it: only_option = list(distances[city].keys())[0] and return only_option, distances[city][only_option].
Update the docstrings of all three helpers, and the DESTINATION HELPERS section comment, so they describe the dictionary version instead of parallel lists.
